title: Do open permit records predict how long a permit and the build behind it take, better than each city's own averages?
lede: research programme: LightGBM quantile models beat the per-city, per-type empirical-quantile baseline on pinball loss in 13 of 15 city/target/quantile cells (2024 test year, Chicago, San Francisco, Austin); Chicago's tails are the exception
summary: An open research programme on duration forecasting from public building-permit feeds. Session 1 wrote the proposal (12 checked works, four falsifiable hypotheses, time-split evaluation with conformal intervals) and probed the feeds: Chicago has 851,778 rows, all issued, so it cannot show permits never issued; San Francisco has 1,297,657 rows with 750,188 completed; Austin has 2,382,939 rows with 2,184,191 completed. NYC DOB NOW is excluded until its licence is checked. Session 2 built the loader, schema, datasheets and a manifest (row counts match the probe) and found the median application-to-issue lag is 0 days in all three cities (p90 56, 81, 142), with SF and Austin build times at a median of about 105 days. Session 5 ran the reference-class baselines on the real feeds; session 6 (milestone 3) fitted LightGBM quantile models (q 0.1, 0.5, 0.9) and a same-day classifier, forward split with train to 2022 and early stopping on 2023, tested on 2024. The boosted model beats the baseline in 13 of 15 city/target/quantile cells by 2 to 36% (paired week-block bootstrap intervals exclude zero); in Chicago application-to-issue it wins at the median and loses at the 0.1 and 0.9 quantiles. One test year, 3 seeds, fixed fast configuration, intervals not yet conformalised. Session 78 scored build time on Seattle test years old enough to be seen in full (2020 to 2022): folding demolition into alteration costs 1.7 to 2.5 days at the 0.9 quantile (95% intervals above zero), while complete-case scoring of a two-year window reverses that sign in two of three years, and inverse-probability-of-censoring weights recover only 10 to 40% of the gap because 5 to 8% of each cohort outlasts the window. The earlier fold gain is withdrawn as a censoring artefact; the transfer model's median gain stands. Session 79 ran the work-type class itself on the same mature cohorts: it lowers Seattle's build-time 0.9-quantile transfer loss by 3.2 to 6.3 days in every year (so the 2.2-day cost reported earlier was censoring too), and San Francisco's by 15.7 days, but raises Austin's by 15.3; folding demolition helps Austin by 2.0 days in 2021 (not in 2020, where it costs 1.8) and does nothing in San Francisco. Session 80 found the city signs hold in 2020 and 2022 (San Francisco +14.4 and +22.7 days, Austin −17.2 and −9.8) and traced both to which classes the source cities fill. Under permit type alone the sources have no rows in the held-out city's main classes; the work-type class fills San Francisco's alteration class (98% of its permits) with 271,672 source rows, but fills Austin's electrical, mechanical and plumbing classes (76% of its permits, 77 to 86% of the cost) with only 42 to 466 Seattle rows whose 0.9-quantile build times are 1.6 to 2.7 times Austin's own. Session 81 tested a minimum-support rule fixed in advance: a class with fewer than 1,000 source training rows (k chosen on 2020) is folded into “other”. In 2021 and 2022 it wins back 9.3 and 4.6 days of Austin's 0.9-quantile cost (61% and 47%) and keeps San Francisco's and Seattle's gains. But it costs Austin 8.5 and 4.4 days at the median: a folded class shares the sources' catch-all durations instead of staying unseen. Session 82 tried the other fold targets: folding those classes to a missing class removes the median cost but gives back the tail (−1.2 and +1.1 days at q0.9), because the sources' thin-class rows, now NaN, still train the branch LightGBM shares between missing and never-seen categories; dropping those rows recovers the tail (−13.0 and −5.4) and brings the median cost back. Across all four treatments the plain permit-type class still wins in Austin, so the class configuration must be chosen per target city. Session 83 did that from the target's own previous year, scored with the transfer model that never saw it: across 12 city-year-quantile cells the pick lands within 0.65 days of the best of three candidates (mean regret 0.07 days, against 1.7 to 6.6 for any fixed class). Session 84 scored that choice on the labels a deployment has on 1 January of the test year, when only 28 to 61% of the target's previous-year permits have completed: mean regret rises to 1.1 to 1.6 days; the best deployable variant (two years back, inverse-probability-of-censoring weights, a significance gate) reaches 0.58 days, within a day of the best in 11 of 12 cells. Its one miss is Seattle's 0.9 quantile, where the permits already completed favour the plain permit type (interval below zero) while the full cohort favours the work-type class by 4.8 days: censoring bias that a significance gate cannot catch. Session 85 chose from the target's year Y-3 (93 to 99% complete on 1 January) and early-stopped the borrowed model on only the source permits completed by then: the selector's mean regret falls to 0.31 days and Seattle's miss goes, but the early-stopping cut raises the best candidate's loss by 1.3 days on average (up to 6.9 days in Austin's 0.9 quantile), more than the selector's whole regret. Session 86 built the borrowed model only from what was known on 1 January: training rows cut to permits completed by then (under 1.3% removed) and each quantile's boosting rounds fixed from older years (trained to Y-4, early-stopped on Y-3). Austin's 0.9-quantile loss is back within 0.8 days of the complete-label model, but the 0.9-quantile models stop after 7 to 28 rounds and the best candidate's loss rises by 1.86 days on average (10.9 in Seattle 2021), worse than session 85; the selector still lands within 0.36 days of the best, which pointed at how many rounds the tail model gets. Session 87 tested that and it does not hold: early-stopping on the sources' year Y-3 directly still stops the 0.9-quantile models after 8 to 17 rounds (34 to 121 with complete labels), yet the round count does not track the tail loss across 18 model-cells (Spearman 0.02). Cutting the training rows to permits finished by 1 January, only 0.45 to 0.56% of them, alone costs San Francisco and Seattle 1.0 to 5.1 days at the 0.9 quantile, 44 to 92% of the deployable model's cost there: the open part is the longest builds, still unfinished on the decision date. Session 88 weighted the finished source permits by the inverse chance of having finished by 1 January (IPCW): in the deployable model the weights halve San Francisco and Seattle's 0.9-quantile cost (+2.53 days against the complete-label model, unweighted +4.74; better in 4 of 4 city-years), but they give back only 18 to 33% of the training cut's cost, because 55 to 65% of the dropped permits outlast every window their city-year has on that date, which only a censored-tail model can reach. Session 89 tried that with Portnoy’s censored-quantile pseudo-rows (open permits split between their window and “+infinity” above a Kaplan-Meier level): the tail cost rose to +36.4 days (cut variant) and +84.9 (deployable), because LightGBM’s quantile leaf renewal sets a leaf to a weighted percentile of its residuals and so lands on the pseudo-rows’ far-right labels; capping them at the longest completed build still gives +21.8 and +14.5 days and predictions up to 25,600 days. All ten predictions refuted; Session 90 replaced the pseudo-rows with a censored pinball objective (an open permit charged only while the prediction is below its window, each leaf set to that loss’s own minimiser): the deployable model’s 0.9-quantile cost in San Francisco and Seattle falls to +1.63 days (IPCW +2.53, unweighted +4.74; better than IPCW in 4 of 4 city-years), with predictions past ten years on at most three test permits in 3 of 24 runs. Session 91 put back the permits the feeds never mark complete (39% of San Francisco’s issued permits, 23% of Seattle’s, flat by year back to 2010; in San Francisco mostly still “issued” or “expired”, records nobody closed out): read as lower bounds they cost the borrowed tail model +181 days at q0.9, but dropping any open more than five years on the decision date gives the first deployable variant to match the complete-label model (−0.41 days on average; Seattle better by 5.7 to 6.9 days, San Francisco worse by 1.6 to 2.9). Session 92 swept that threshold (2, 3, 5, 8 years): 3 years is best in San Francisco, 5 in Seattle, and 3 years is the most robust fixed choice over six city-years with Austin (q0.9 −0.80 days on average, worst +1.50); but choosing it by the censored loss on the sources’ older permits as seen on the decision date picks 8 years every time (mean regret 11.3 days in San Francisco and Seattle, 60 to 68 in Austin), because never-closed records reward any model that predicts long. Session 94 audited the labels: completion dates are builds, not administrative closures (0.04% of dated completions in San Francisco, 0.4% in Seattle, 1.5% in Austin sit on permits the status calls expired, void or withdrawn), while 71% of Seattle’s undated “Completed” permits say “Closed as Incomplete”, so they never finished. Session 95 dropped those dead completions from the borrowed model’s training: over the whole history they are 6.5 to 8.6% of rows, because 96% of Austin’s void and expired permits issued before 2000 carry a completion date exactly 180 days after issue (an expiry stamp, the commonest build-time label in Austin’s feed, 143,212 rows). Removing them lengthens the 0.9-quantile tail and costs Seattle 1.8 to 3.5 days while San Francisco does not move, so the closures were not what held the deployable model back. Session 96 split that drop: the 180-day stamps are 82 to 83% of the dropped rows, yet dropping only them moves the 0.9-quantile loss by +0.64 days on average, within seed noise in 3 of 4 cells. Seattle’s cost comes from the other closures, mostly Austin’s withdrawn permits with long durations (worse without them in 6 of 6 seeds), which help San Francisco (better without them in 5 of 6). The staleness cut keeps its city pattern on clean sources: 3 years in San Francisco, 5 in Seattle. Session 97 dropped as many live permits of the same lengths instead (a placebo): it reproduces most of San Francisco’s gain and about half of Seattle’s cost, so the closures matter mostly for the long-tail label mass they carry, not for being closures. Session 98 let the target city choose among those source rules from its own permits issued three years earlier: scored on the ones completed by the decision date it picks the 3-year cut everywhere (mean regret 2.35 days, 5.46 in Seattle 2021), scored by the censored loss the 5-year stamp rule everywhere (regret 1.79), and the fixed 5-year cut beats both, so neither score a deployment holds carries the city signal yet. Session 99 found one that does: scored on the target’s own permits issued six years earlier and completed by the decision date, the selector picks the 3-year cut in San Francisco and the 5-year cut in Seattle, the best rule in all four city-years (regret 0, mean q0.9 71.12 days against the best fixed rule’s 72.27); five-year-old permits get three of four, and IPCW on the three-year-old ones does not cross, since their follow-up stops at the shorter cut. Four cells and sub-day Seattle margins make this a rule to test further. Session 100 tested it on six new cells and it did not replicate: in test years 2019 and 2020 a 5-year rule beats the 3-year cut in San Francisco and Seattle alike, yet every target-cohort score (3, 5, 6 or 8 years old, plain or IPCW) still picks the 3-year cut (mean regret 2.15 days against 0.12 for the fixed 5-year cut); with Austin as the target the 3-year cut wins by about 16 days and every selector finds it. The earlier 4 of 4 was the selector agreeing with a city split that holds only in the years the rules were tuned on. Session 101 refit all eight San Francisco and Seattle city-years with per-permit predictions and bootstrapped them: at least 96% of resamples keep each pick on the same side and every test-year interval excludes zero, so the selector is stably wrong, not noisy; an independent rerun reproduced session 100 to the digit. Session 102 added test years 2017 and 2018, and they side with 2021 and 2022: the 3-year cut beats the 5-year cut in San Francisco by 8.86 and 2.94 days and in Seattle 2017, and the six-year-old-permit selector picks it in all four (regret 0.29 days). Pooled over all twelve San Francisco and Seattle city-years 2017 to 2022 (post hoc), the selector leaves 0.81 days of regret against 1.53 for the best fixed rule, so its failures concentrate in 2019 and 2020; a 4-year cut is the best fixed rule in the early years and a 6-year cut costs 7.5 days. Session 103 fit the 4-year cut in 2019 to 2022 too: pooled over the twelve city-years it leaves 0.78 days of regret against the best of the 3-, 4- and 5-year cuts (5-year 1.67, 3-year 1.73, the six-year-old-permit chooser 0.91), is never the worst of the three, and misses by at most 2.31 days (5-year cut 8.86), so it is the robust default for borrowing other cities' permits, though the 5-year cut still edges it in 2019 to 2022 alone (78.16 against 78.48 days). Session 104 tried a staleness cut set from each source city’s own recent completions (0.99 quantile of build days over the last 3 years): it left 6.65 days of mean q0.9 regret against 0.78 for a fixed 4-year cut, because a 2017 Seattle close-out batch of 467 permits older than 8 years pushed Seattle’s quantile to 10.3 years for three forecast years; the fixed 4-year cut stays the default. Session 105 tried two robust per-source cuts fixed in advance (the 0.95 quantile of recent completions; the 0.99 quantile with batch close-out days dropped): 2.51 and 2.00 days of mean q0.9 regret against 0.78 for the fixed 4-year cut. The short rule suits San Francisco as target and the batch-dropped rule Seattle, a target dependence no statistic of the source cities can see, so the fixed 4-year cut stays the default. Session 106 tested that default with Austin as target (shorter builds than its sources SF and Seattle) in 2017 to 2022: the 3-year cut wins all six years and the 4-year cut gives up 12.74 days of q0.9 (5-year 18.12); pooled over 18 city-years the 3-year cut leaves 1.16 days of regret against 4.77, and choosing among the 3-, 4- and 5-year cuts by the target’s own six-year-old permits leaves 0.61 (worst city-year 4.44). The advice changes: score the cuts on the target’s six-year-old permits, or use the 3-year cut without that history. Session 108 fitted the 1-year cut (completed source builds only) for San Francisco and Seattle as target: there it is barely worse than the 2-year cut (0.65 days of mean q0.9, against 3.32 from 2 to 3 years), so the menu has two regimes, completed builds only and a 3- to 5-year allowance. Choosing among the 1- to 5-year cuts by the target’s six-year-old permits leaves 1.62 days of pooled regret over 18 city-years (2- to 5-year chooser 2.38, best fixed cut, 3 years, 3.27; worst city-year 6.03), all of the gain from Austin; in San Francisco and Seattle it costs 0.21 days a city-year, because it still leans short in SF 2017 to 2021.
